content: Necatoriasis is an infection caused by Necator hookworms, particularly Necator americanus. This condition is classified as a helminthic infection and is considered a neglected tropical disease. When adult Necator worms attach to the villi of the small intestine, they feed on the host's blood. This can result in symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, cramps, and weight loss, which may progress to anorexia. In cases of heavy infection, significant blood loss can lead to iron deficiency and hypochromic microcytic anemia. In children, this type of anemia can cause both physical and mental developmental delays. Additionally, the infection can manifest as cutaneous larva migrans, a skin condition characterized by severe itching and skin lesions. The causative agent, Necator americanus, has two main life stages: larvae and adult worms. The third-stage larvae are attracted to human skin by thermal gradients. They typically penetrate the skin of the hands or feet upon contact with contaminated soil. At the site of entry, a papular, itchy rash known as ground itch develops. During their migration through the lungs, symptoms are usually absent, but mild coughing and throat irritation may occur. Once the larvae reach the alveoli, they are swallowed and enter the gastrointestinal tract, where they attach to the intestinal mucosa and mature into adult worms. Using their cutting plates, the worms penetrate blood vessels and feed on the host's blood, consuming approximately 30 μL of blood per worm per day. This blood loss is the primary cause of iron-deficiency anemia in moderate to heavy infections. Other symptoms include epigastric pain, nausea, fatigue, headache, exertional shortness of breath, joint pain, sternal pain, and, in some cases, impotence. Death from necatoriasis is rare. Diagnosis of necatoriasis is typically achieved by identifying N. americanus eggs in a stool sample under a microscope. However, in cases of light infection, eggs may be difficult to detect, necessitating the use of concentration techniques such as flotation or sedimentation. It is important to note that the eggs of Ancylostoma duodenale and N. americanus are indistinguishable, so larval examination is required for definitive identification. Larvae are not usually present in stool samples unless the sample has been left at room temperature for an extended period. The most common diagnostic method involves fixing the stool sample in 10% formalin, concentrating it using the formalin-ethyl acetate sedimentation technique, and preparing a wet mount of the sediment for microscopic examination. Preventing necatoriasis involves education, improved sanitation, and proper disposal of human feces. Treatment for N. americanus infection typically involves the use of benzimidazole-class anthelmintics such as albendazole or mebendazole. In severe cases of anemia, a blood transfusion may be required. Light infections are often left untreated in areas where reinfection is common. Iron supplementation and a protein-rich diet can aid in recovery. Studies have shown that albendazole is more effective than mebendazole for treating N. americanus infections, with a cure rate of 95% compared to 21% for mebendazole. Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen has been used to treat cutaneous larva migrans, but this method is associated with significant pain and skin damage and is now largely replaced by pharmaceutical treatments. Topical medications may be used but require repeated applications and are generally less effective than systemic treatments. The preferred antimicrobial regimen for N. americanus is a single oral dose of albendazole 400 mg. Alternative regimens include mebendazole (100 mg orally twice daily or 500 mg daily for three days) or pyrantel pamoate (11 mg/kg orally once daily, up to a maximum of 1 g/day, for three days). Necator americanus was first identified in Brazil and later discovered in Texas. It is now known to be endemic in Africa, China, the southwest Pacific islands, India, and Southeast Asia. This parasite thrives in tropical climates and is the most common hookworm species infecting humans. In the southern United States, approximately 95% of hookworm infections are caused by N. americanus. While primarily a human parasite, it can also infect pigs and dogs. Transmission requires the deposition of feces containing eggs onto warm, humid, well-drained soil, where direct contact with contaminated soil facilitates infection.
